power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective: To describe the role of hysterectomy in modifying the major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors.
Hysterectomy is the surgical removal of the uterus [1].
text.formatted: Hysterectomy is the surgical removal of the uterus <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: It is one of the most common gynecological procedures, with estimates of 0.6 million women undergoing hysterectomy annually in the United States [2].
text.formatted: It is one of the most common gynecological procedures, with estimates of 0.6 million women undergoing hysterectomy annually in the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Around 90% of surgeries are conducted to manage benign gynecological conditions like abnormal uterine bleeding, endometriosis, and uterine fibroids, where approximately 44% undergo concomitant bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as part of the treatment process or to mitigate the risk of ovarian malignancy [3].
text.formatted: Around 90% of surgeries are conducted to manage benign gynecological conditions like abnormal uterine bleeding, endometriosis, and uterine fibroids, where approximately 44% undergo concomitant bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as part of the treatment process or to mitigate the risk of ovarian malignancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Although the treatment approaches for benign gynecological conditions have significantly evolved, hysterectomies are still increasingly performed owing to their low perioperative morbidity and rapid therapeutic effects [4].
text.formatted: Although the treatment approaches for benign gynecological conditions have significantly evolved, hysterectomies are still increasingly performed owing to their low perioperative morbidity and rapid therapeutic effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Emerging evidence from recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggests a positive epidemiological association between hysterectomy (even with ovarian conservation) and increased long-term cardiovascular disease risk [4] [5] [6].
text.formatted: Emerging evidence from recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggests a positive epidemiological association between hysterectomy (even with ovarian conservation) and increased long-term cardiovascular disease risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: However, the data don't emphasize specific pathophysiological mechanisms, making it difficult to distinguish chance from causation [4, 5].
text.formatted: However, the data don't emphasize specific pathophysiological mechanisms, making it difficult to distinguish chance from causation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: Cardiovascular risk factors are multifactorial, and some are modifiable [7] [8] [9] [10].
text.formatted: Cardiovascular risk factors are multifactorial, and some are modifiable <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Puri et al. classify cardiovascular risk factors as major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors, high-risk features, and risk modifiers [8].
text.formatted: Puri et al. classify cardiovascular risk factors as major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors, high-risk features, and risk modifiers <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Major ASCVD risk factors include age ≥ 45 in males and ≥ 55 in females, current cigarette smoking or tobacco use, and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL) [8].
text.formatted: Major ASCVD risk factors include age ≥ 45 in males and ≥ 55 in females, current cigarette smoking or tobacco use, and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Family history of premature ASCVD, chronic kidney disease stage 3B or 4, apolipoprotein B > 130 mg/dl, extreme elevation of a single risk factor, lipoprotein (a) ≥ 50 mg/dl, metabolic syndrome, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease with grade two or three fibrosis, and a coronary artery calcium score < 75th percentile are among high-risk features [7, 8].
text.formatted: Family history of premature ASCVD, chronic kidney disease stage 3B or 4, apolipoprotein B > 130 mg/dl, extreme elevation of a single risk factor, lipoprotein (a) ≥ 50 mg/dl, metabolic syndrome, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease with grade two or three fibrosis, and a coronary artery calcium score < 75th percentile are among high-risk features <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Risk modifiers include lipoprotein a 20-40 mg/dl, impaired fasting glucose (100-125 mg/dl), increased waist circumference (> 90 cm in men and > 80 cm in women), high sensitivity C-reactive protein > 2mg/L, plasma triglyceride > 150 mg/dl (fasting), rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, spondyloarthritis, premature menopause, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, polycystic ovarian syndrome, high polygenic risk score, air pollution and human immunodeficiency virus [8, 10].
text.formatted: Risk modifiers include lipoprotein a 20-40 mg/dl, impaired fasting glucose (100-125 mg/dl), increased waist circumference (> 90 cm in men and > 80 cm in women), high sensitivity C-reactive protein > 2mg/L, plasma triglyceride > 150 mg/dl (fasting), rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, spondyloarthritis, premature menopause, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, polycystic ovarian syndrome, high polygenic risk score, air pollution and human immunodeficiency virus <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: To comprehensively evaluate the association between hysterectomy and cardiovascular risk, we need to establish the correlation between hysterectomy and the well-established cardiovascular risk factors.

As it was not feasible to analyze every risk factor within the categories listed above, we selected five main risk factors in accordance with the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines [7, 9, 10].
text.formatted: As it was not feasible to analyze every risk factor within the categories listed above, we selected five main risk factors in accordance with the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: If these five show a stronger association, we can then analyze additional factors.
ESC guidelines describe the main causal and modifiable ASCVD risk factors as cholesterol (apo-B-containing lipoproteins), hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, and adiposity [9].
text.formatted: ESC guidelines describe the main causal and modifiable ASCVD risk factors as cholesterol (apo-B-containing lipoproteins), hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, and adiposity <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize evidence on the role of hysterectomy in modifying the main modifiable ASCVD risk factors.
However, a long process of data exploration, synthesis, and analysis precedes classifying hysterectomy as a 'high-risk feature' or 'risk modifier'.
This review will ultimately shift how hysterectomy is viewed, from a gynecological procedure to a broader medical intervention.
We retrieved the relevant studies from PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ScienceDirect, published up to March 10, 2026.
text.formatted: We retrieved the relevant studies from PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ScienceDirect, published up to <ref type="bibr">March 10, 2026</ref>.

text.text: The search strings included "Hysterectomy", "Cardiovascular disease", "Coronary artery disease", "Heart disease", "Ischemic heart disease", "Cardiovascular risk", "Cardiac morbidity", "Coronary heart disease", "Diabetes", "Hypertension", "Dyslipidemia", "Hyperlipidemia", "Metabolic syndrome", "Metabolic morbidity" which were combined using Boolean expressions "AND," "OR" to form precise search queries.
A detailed line-by-line search strategy is given in S1 File.
The study selection process was conducted in a blinded, two-step approach using the semiautomated tool Rayyan [11], involving two independent reviewers (TDKMJ) and (DMCSJ).
text.formatted: The study selection process was conducted in a blinded, two-step approach using the semiautomated tool Rayyan <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, involving two independent reviewers (TDKMJ) and (DMCSJ).

text.text: In the first round, title and abstract screening removed duplicates, with conflicts resolved by (SDS); similarly, the second round used a similar blinded approach for full-text screening, with conflicts resolved by (AJ).
The study selection process followed the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram for updated systematic reviews [12].
text.formatted: The study selection process followed the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram for updated systematic reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: The current study protocol was prospectively registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO CRD420251241667).
• Articles reporting cardiovascular events and new-onset diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and other metabolic effects following hysterectomy.
• Full-text articles in the English language • Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, case series, and experimental studies.
• Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, or book chapters.
Two reviewers (DMCSJ & AJ) conducted the initial data extraction independently, and a third reviewer (SS) cross-checked it.

text.text: We performed separate meta-analyses using a generic inverse-variance model with random effects for each outcome, stratifying by study design (cross-sectional vs. cohort) and effect measure (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], or relative risk [RR]).

text.text: For each study, we calculated the log-transformed effect estimate and its standard error from the reported 95% confidence intervals and entered them into RevMan.
We assessed heterogeneity using the I² statistic; I² values ≥ 50% were considered high heterogeneity.

When a single study reported multiple exposure groups (e.g., hysterectomy alone vs. hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy) sharing the same reference group, we pooled these estimates internally before inclusion.
We performed sensitivity analyses by excluding larger studies to assess their influence on pooled estimates.
We assessed publication bias using funnel plot asymmetry.

We excluded studies from quantitative synthesis if they reported no measure of association (aOR, aHR, or RR) with 95% confidence intervals, or if there was only one study per outcome and no comparable studies for pooling.
We performed narrative synthesis for outcomes that did not meet metaanalysis criteria.
All pooled estimates are presented as summary effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals, accompanied by forest plots.
Results were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05.

text.text: The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) assessed the cohort studies and rated all as high quality.
The modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessed the cross-sectional studies and rated them as average to good quality.
Visual assessment of the publication bias revealed minimal asymmetry in the funnel plot.
Pooled evidence from cross-sectional and cohort studies showed that hysterectomy is associated with a 19% to 32% increased risk of hypertension.
Pooled evidence from both cross-sectional studies and cohort studies reported that hysterectomy is associated with around a 20% increase in the odds of diabetes.
Meta-analysis of cohort studies revealed that hysterectomy increased the risk of hyperlipidemia by 21%.
Cross-sectional studies found that hysterectomy was associated with a 24% increase in the odds of both obesity and metabolic syndrome.
In the largest study, Bi et al. reported that hysterectomy was associated with a 25% increased risk of MAFLD, analyzing over 9 million urban Chinese women [29].

text.text: Premature ovarian failure is the most widely proposed explanation for the observed associations between hysterectomy and cardiovascular risk factors [2, 20, 23, 24, 27, 29].

text.text: The ovarian blood supply is derived from both the ovarian and uterine arteries via the utero-ovarian anastomosis.
Ligation of the uterine vessels during hysterectomy may significantly reduce ovarian perfusion [31].
text.formatted: Ligation of the uterine vessels during hysterectomy may significantly reduce ovarian perfusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, even when the ovaries are preserved, hysterectomy may compromise ovarian function, which may explain why women who undergo hysterectomy with ovarian conservation experience earlier menopause compared to women with intact uteri [3, 31].
text.formatted: Therefore, even when the ovaries are preserved, hysterectomy may compromise ovarian function, which may explain why women who undergo hysterectomy with ovarian conservation experience earlier menopause compared to women with intact uteri <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31]</ref>.

text.text: Ovarian dysfunction leads to reduced levels of estrogen and other ovarian hormones with systemic metabolic consequences [17].
text.formatted: Ovarian dysfunction leads to reduced levels of estrogen and other ovarian hormones with systemic metabolic consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Adverse cardio-metabolic effects seen in premature ovarian failure are primarily due to estrogen deficiency.

Estrogen contributes to glucose homeostasis by enhancing insulin sensitivity, promoting insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, facilitating glucose uptake via GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane, and suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis [16, 23].
text.formatted: Estrogen contributes to glucose homeostasis by enhancing insulin sensitivity, promoting insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, facilitating glucose uptake via GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane, and suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: The abrupt decline in estrogen following hysterectomy in premenopausal women may precipitate insulin resistance and increase diabetes risk.
Estrogen plays a role in lipid metabolism by increasing HDL-cholesterol, decreasing LDL-cholesterol, and reducing lipoprotein (a) levels [15, 30].
text.formatted: Estrogen plays a role in lipid metabolism by increasing HDL-cholesterol, decreasing LDL-cholesterol, and reducing lipoprotein (a) levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>.

text.text: Estrogen also promotes blood pressure regulation by increasing nitric oxide bioavailability, inhibiting vascular smooth muscle proliferation, reducing angiotensin II receptor expression, and modulating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system [2, 28].
text.formatted: Estrogen also promotes blood pressure regulation by increasing nitric oxide bioavailability, inhibiting vascular smooth muscle proliferation, reducing angiotensin II receptor expression, and modulating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>.

text.text: The loss of these protective effects following hysterectomy may predispose women to hypertension.
Estrogen also plays a role in obesity and metabolic syndrome through its effects on central appetite regulation, adipose tissue distribution, and adipocyte metabolism [28].
text.formatted: Estrogen also plays a role in obesity and metabolic syndrome through its effects on central appetite regulation, adipose tissue distribution, and adipocyte metabolism <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: None of the included studies directly assessed postoperative ovarian function following hysterectomy with ovarian conservation.
The physical presence of ovaries does not necessarily equate to functional ovaries, as the disruption of the utero-ovarian vascular supply may render conserved ovaries functionally compromised.
This may explain why hysterectomy alone (without oophorectomy) consistently demonstrated positive associations with adverse metabolic outcomes.
In addition, the relatively smaller sample sizes in the hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy groups limited the statistical power to detect the additional risk attributable to oophorectomy.

Therefore, our meta-analytic approach combined the two groups to maximize statistical power while acknowledging that hysterectomy, regardless of ovarian conservation, appears to confer cardiovascular risk.
Some studies have shown that bilateral oophorectomy alone (without hysterectomy) does not increase cardiovascular risk factors and, in some cases, may even be protective [3, 23, 31].
text.formatted: Some studies have shown that bilateral oophorectomy alone (without hysterectomy) does not increase cardiovascular risk factors and, in some cases, may even be protective <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31]</ref>.

text.text: These findings may reflect the dual hormonal effects of oophorectomy.
Bilateral oophorectomy reduces not only estrogen production but also androgen production (particularly testosterone).
The ovaries contribute approximately 50% of circulating testosterone in premenopausal women [3, 23].
text.formatted: The ovaries contribute approximately 50% of circulating testosterone in premenopausal women <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: While estrogen deficiency increases the risk of diabetes and metabolic dysfunction, reduced androgen levels may mitigate or even reverse this risk [3, 23].
text.formatted: While estrogen deficiency increases the risk of diabetes and metabolic dysfunction, reduced androgen levels may mitigate or even reverse this risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: In cases of hysterectomy alone with ovarian preservation, the extent of reduction in androgen and estrogen production due to vascular compromise may vary.
Compromise of ovarian function with retention of androgen production can result in more pronounced metabolic effects than bilateral oophorectomy.
Therefore, consider both postoperative estrogen and androgen levels when interpreting these findings.
Multiple studies have shown that the association between hysterectomy and cardiovascular risk factors is more pronounced among younger women [2, 3, 19, 20, 23, 24].

text.text: Madika et al. reported that the risk of hypertension increased with earlier age at hysterectomy, with a hazard ratio of 1.28 (95% CI: 1.13-1.45) for women under 40 years compared to 1.12 (95% CI: 1.03-1.22) for women over 50 years (p < 0.0001) [19].

text.text: Chiang et al. reported that women aged 30-39 years who underwent hysterectomy had a hazard ratio of 1.75 (95% CI: 1.27-2.41) for diabetes, compared with 1.33 (95% CI: 1.19-1.49) for women aged 40-49 years [24].

text.text: Increasing age itself is a well-recognized cardiovascular risk factor.
The risk is relatively low in younger females [8].
text.formatted: The risk is relatively low in younger females <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: When younger females undergo hysterectomy ± oophorectomy, they are compared with younger control groups, revealing the cardiovascular risk attributable to hysterectomy.

However, increasing age may have overridden the cardiovascular risk attributable to hysterectomy in older females, showing no statistically significant difference between those who underwent surgery and control groups.
In younger women, the ovaries still produce significant amounts of estrogen and other hormones.
The abrupt loss of these hormones may be more metabolically disruptive than in older women.
Clinicians should be aware of the potential long-term cardiovascular consequences in women who undergo hysterectomy at younger ages.
This is particularly important given that younger women may not typically be considered at high cardiovascular risk and may not receive routine screening for metabolic conditions.
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is often prescribed to manage menopausal symptoms, particularly for younger women who experience surgical menopause.
However, most of the included studies did not report data on HRT use, which may be a significant source of both confounding and effect modification [2, 18, 20, 23, 28, 29, 32].

text.text: Ouyang et al. addressed this issue most directly in their UK Biobank analysis.

They found that HRT use in women who had undergone hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy was not associated with increased diabetes risk (hysterectomy alone: aHR1.01, 95% CI:0.84-1.21; hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy: aHR1.03, 95% CI:0.83-1.28) [23].

text.text: The lack of association may reflect exogenous hormones attenuating post-surgery hormonal changes.
Several other studies adjusted for HRT use but did not provide detailed analyses of how HRT modified the associations [3, 16, 19, 20, 22].

text.text: Premenopausal women experience regular menstrual blood loss, which leads to lower levels of stored iron (ferritin) and hemoglobin compared with men and postmenopausal women [20, 25].
text.formatted: Premenopausal women experience regular menstrual blood loss, which leads to lower levels of stored iron (ferritin) and hemoglobin compared with men and postmenopausal women <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: This relative iron deficiency has been proposed as a protective factor against cardiovascular disease.
Excess iron promotes oxidative stress, catalyzing the production of highly reactive hydroxyl radicals that can oxidize LDL-cholesterol and promote atherosclerosis [20, 25].
text.formatted: Excess iron promotes oxidative stress, catalyzing the production of highly reactive hydroxyl radicals that can oxidize LDL-cholesterol and promote atherosclerosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: Hysterectomy permanently eliminates this physiological mechanism of iron loss, leading to an early increase in hematocrit and iron stores [20].
text.formatted: Hysterectomy permanently eliminates this physiological mechanism of iron loss, leading to an early increase in hematocrit and iron stores <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Elevated hematocrit increases whole-blood viscosity, leading to endothelial dysfunction and subsequent hypertension [20].
text.formatted: Elevated hematocrit increases whole-blood viscosity, leading to endothelial dysfunction and subsequent hypertension <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Yuk et al. found that the risk of hypertension following hysterectomy was significantly higher only in women whose hemoglobin increased by 2 g/dL or more after surgery (aHR1.34, 95% CI:1.22-1.42).
The proportion of women with a hemoglobin increase of ≥2 g/dL was significantly higher in the hysterectomy group (35.7%) compared to the non-hysterectomy group (8.2%, p<0.001) [20].
text.formatted: The proportion of women with a hemoglobin increase of ≥2 g/dL was significantly higher in the hysterectomy group (35.7%) compared to the non-hysterectomy group (8.2%, p<0.001) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that even when ovarian function is preserved, the cessation of menstrual bleeding may independently increase cardiovascular risk through ironmediated pathways.
However, as heavy menstrual bleeding is a common indication for hysterectomy, post-hysterectomy hemoglobin rise is an expected outcome.
These findings may reflect confounding.
Therefore, it is difficult to arrive at clinical decisions.

To identify clinically meaningful differences in cardiovascular risk, RCTs should compare hysterectomy versus a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG/IUS) in patients with heavy menstrual bleeding.
The uterus may have endocrine or paracrine functions beyond its reproductive role, which can potentially mitigate cardiovascular risk factors.
Hysterectomy may eliminate these protective functions even when the ovaries are conserved.
Only a few studies have examined the association between hysterectomy performed after menopause and cardiovascular risk factors.
The existing evidence is inadequate because of relatively small sample sizes [17, 19, 21, 25, 30, 31].

text.text: Laughlin-Tommaso et al. found that women who underwent hysterectomy after age 50 did not have any added risk.
However, their sample size in this age stratum was relatively small (271 vs 4,188), limiting the power to detect moderate associations [18].

text.text: The possibility that the uterus produces a substance (such as prostacyclin, prostaglandin, relaxin, various growth factors, or cytokines) that protects against cardiovascular disease even after menopause warrants further investigation [25].

text.text: Some studies raise the concern that the same conditions that lead to hysterectomy may also increase cardiovascular risk factors, referred to as "confounding by indication".
The most common indications for hysterectomy, like uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and abnormal uterine bleeding, may themselves be associated with metabolic risk factors.
Uterine fibroids are more common in women with obesity, hypertension, and diabetes [29].
text.formatted: Uterine fibroids are more common in women with obesity, hypertension, and diabetes <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: The mechanisms linking fibroids to these conditions may involve shared inflammatory pathways, insulin resistance, and hormonal influences.
Endometriosis is associated with chronic systemic inflammation, which may also increase the risk of hypertension through endothelial dysfunction and vascular inflammation [19].
text.formatted: Endometriosis is associated with chronic systemic inflammation, which may also increase the risk of hypertension through endothelial dysfunction and vascular inflammation <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, women who undergo hysterectomy may already have a higher baseline cardiovascular risk profile that precedes the surgery.

Madika et al. found that endometriosis (aHR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.11-1.22) and fibroids (aHR 1.18, 95% CI: 1.13-1.22) were both independently associated with hypertension, even after adjustment for hysterectomy status and other confounders.
Women with both hysterectomy and endometriosis had the highest risk (aHR 1.24, 95% CI: 1.11-1.38) [19].

text.text: This is a critical limitation because reverse causation, where pre-existing metabolic risk factors increase the likelihood of hysterectomy, cannot be ruled out.

There is a possibility that women who undergo hysterectomy have more frequent contact with healthcare providers and are therefore more likely to be diagnosed with cardiovascular risk factors compared to women with intact uteri.
This bias could inflate the apparent association between hysterectomy and metabolic outcomes by increasing the detection rate.
Ding et al. found that the number of clinic visits and hospitalizations was higher in the hysterectomy group than in the comparison group, raising the possibility of surveillance bias [17].

text.text: Surveillance bias cannot be entirely ruled out, particularly in studies that rely on administrative databases, where diagnoses are recorded from clinical encounters rather than systematic screening.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive systematic review and metaanalysis specifically designed to evaluate the role of hysterectomy in modifying the main modifiable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors as defined by the European Society of Cardiology guidelines.
The inclusion of studies from diverse populations, including American, European, Korean, Taiwanese, Chinese, Indian, and multi-ethnic cohorts, enhances the generalizability of the findings.
The inclusion of high-quality studies strengthened the evidence.
Despite these strengths, several limitations remain.
Heterogeneity across studies was substantial, so the pooled estimates should be interpreted with caution.

We were unable to perform subgroup analyses comparing hysterectomy alone with hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy, or to assess age at hysterectomy, because few studies provided separate estimates.
The reliance on self-reported hysterectomy status in several studies may introduce bias [2, 16].
text.formatted: The reliance on self-reported hysterectomy status in several studies may introduce bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: Outcome definitions and confounder adjustment varied across studies, affecting comparability.
The lack of data on hormone replacement therapy use is a significant limitation.
The temporality of the association cannot be established with cross-sectional studies, making it difficult to rule out reverse causation.
The studies did not explicitly report the surgical approach to hysterectomy (abdominal, vaginal, or laparoscopic), which may have modified the associations discussed.
The mechanisms linking hysterectomy to cardiovascular risk are not fully understood and warrant further research.
Studies directly measuring ovarian function, hormone levels, and iron status following hysterectomy would help elucidate the relative contributions of these pathways.
Precise documentation of HRT use after hysterectomy is essential to understand its role in modifying cardiovascular risk.
Prospective cohort studies with long follow-up data are needed to establish temporal relationships and quantify the absolute risk associated with hysterectomy at different ages.
Randomized controlled trials comparing hysterectomy with alternatives (such as uterine artery embolization) would provide the strongest evidence of its causal effects.
Mendelian randomization studies with larger sample sizes and more comprehensive genetic data could provide additional evidence of causality.
While hysterectomy provides important benefits for women with symptomatic gynecological conditions, the long-term metabolic consequences should be considered in shared decision-making.
For women who undergo hysterectomy, particularly at a young age, cardiovascular risk factor screening should be initiated early and continued throughout the lifespan.

This systematic review and meta-analysis provide comprehensive evidence that hysterectomy is associated with increased risk of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and metabolic syndrome, which are key modifiable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors.

Multiple pathophysiological mechanisms, including premature ovarian failure, the iron storage hypothesis, cancellation effects of ovarian hormones, and the paracrine or endocrine role of the uterus beyond reproduction, are proposed to describe the biological plausibility of these associations.
There is a need for active cardiovascular risk assessment in women who undergo hysterectomy, particularly at a young age.
Therefore, hysterectomy should not be viewed merely as a gynecological procedure, but rather as a significant modifier of cardiovascular risk.
Future research should further elucidate the mechanisms underlying these associations.
